newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: S.Korean banks move to stop another major collapse.
newsitem.headline: S.Korean banks move to stop another major collapse.

text.p: South Korea's Jinro Ltd has become the latest company to default on debt, but it will stay in business under an agreement by banks to keep struggling firms afloat, the company's main creditor said on Tuesday.
The agreement, reached last week to break a chain of corporate failures that began early this year, called for a temporary freeze on debts owed by major companies.

Jinro Ltd failed to pay back 50.4 billion won ($56.4 million) worth of promissory notes and cheques called in by secondary financial institutions on Monday, an official at the Commercial Bank of Korea said on Tuesday.
The 74-year-old Jinro, which nearly monopolises production of the Korean distilled liquor "soju", is the flagship unit of the Jinro Group, South Korea's 19th largest conglomerate.
Payment defaults usually lead to suspension of all company bank accounts, the first step towards bankruptcy.
The Commercial Bank official said it would not freeze Jinro's bank accounts, despite the default.
Banks last week agreed to continue to extend credit to the 51 largest business groups, even if they defaulted on debt payments, as long as there was hope their operations could be salvaged.
The banks' agreement took effect on Monday, and Jinro was the first company to benefit.
But the decision by the Commercial Bank to keep Jinro's credit lines open sets up a potential battle between leading banks and non-bank financial institutions.

A senior official at the Merchant Banks Association of Korea, representing the nation's 30 merchant banks, told Reuters that merchant banks should be exempted from a clause requiring them to extend additional credits to Jinro.
"We share the basic idea of keeping companies alive. But we can't be institutions obliged to offer additional credits," the official said. He declined to be identified.
"We usually offer short-term loans based only on credit. We can't extend more funds without collateral," he said.
Merchant banks typically make unsecured, short-term loans to companies at relatively high interest rates, mainly by discounting commercial papers and promissory notes.
Commercial banks and other financial institutions with loan exposure to the Jinro Group were due to meet next Monday to discuss future steps.

Analysts said the agreement to continue financing troubled groups was one of the few choices left for local banks, still largely under the government's control. But they said it was a temporary solution.

"Whatever the cause, problems in procedures would eventually lead to problems in the future," said Kim Min-tae, fellow at the private LG Economic Research Institute. "I don't think it will work for a long time."
South Korean financial markets have been rocked by the collapse of two steelmakers this year under crushing debts -- Hanbo Steel Co in January and Sammi Steel Co in March.

Separately on Tuesday, the stock market was also hit by news that textile maker Chung Won Corp was unable to settle promissory notes called in on Monday and now faced a final deadline by the end of Tuesday
Later, a Chung Won official said it had settled repayments on the notes worth 800 million won within the deadline.
Jinro's woes dragged down the stock market. The leading index closed down 9.38 points, or 1.35 percent, to 687.96.
(Conversion: $1 = 893.1 won)
